newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Central African Republic peace deal back on track.
newsitem.headline: Central African Republic peace deal back on track.

text.p: Mali's widely respected former military leader Amadou Toumani Toure has put a Central African Republic peace accord back on track after bloody clashes between African peacekeepers and army dissidents.

But many civilians who fled parts of the capital Bangui where the dissidents held sway have yet to be convinced that a ceasefire deal signed on Wednesday will bring lasting peace following three army mutinies in under a year and ethnic bloodshed.
"The districts that supported the mutineers are almost empty. People there are sceptical," one resident said on Friday. Some began to return, albeit cautiously, at the weekend.
The Red Cross says at least 100 people died in the clashes, which lasted a week.

Relief workers say an estimated 60,000 civilians have fled the capital and are in two camps to the south. Others have returned to their home villages, residents say. Under 10,000 had returned to the capital since the ceasefire.
The army mutinies began over pay and conditions but turned into an bid to topple President Ange-Felix Patasse, a northern civilian elected in 1993. They degenerated into ethnic killings.
African peacekeepers, army dissidents and soldiers loyal to Patasse signed a ceasefire on Wednesday to put the January peace deal back on track after clashes between army dissidents and peacekeepers.
Toumani Toure, architect of the January 25 Bangui Accords, brokered the latest ceasefire.

The seven-point deal envisages the return to barracks of the army dissidents within 10 days and collection of their arms and ammunition, and the creation of patrols formed from all three sides to police their former strongholds.

Toumani Toure and Jean-Marc Simon, the ambassador of France, the former colonial power, undertook to guarantee the individual and collective security of the army dissidents -- provided they handed in their arms within the 10-day deadline.
The ceasefire held firm into the weekend. Peacekeepers patrolled hotspots in the capital.
Toumani Toure and the various sides held talks on Thursday on how the army dissidents would return to barracks and hand in weapons to the French ambassador, who was also present.
Members of an international follow-up committee held weekend meetings to discuss technical points. Fresh substantive talks were scheduled for Monday, sources close to the mediators said.
The clashes between peacekeepers and army dissidents, among a minority who had not rejoined their units under the January deal, followed a June 20 incident between the two sides.
Most of the mutineers were from the Yakoma tribe of former military leader Andre Kolingba.
